title: Local Sparsity Enables Unsupervised LLM Safety Detection
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Each local cluster of points activates only a small, partially overlapping feature subset, so the union stays far smaller than the full dimension.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; dashed lines link clusters to mask bars
description: The left panel is a 2D PCA-style scatter plot with axes PC1 and PC2. It has three colored ellipses labeled Cluster A (blue/purple), Cluster B (green) and Cluster C (orange/red). Each ellipse holds a handful of dark points, and a few gray points are scattered in the background. Dashed lines in each cluster's color run from the ellipses to the right panel. The right panel has three horizontal gray bars, one per cluster, with colored vertical tick marks showing which SAE features that cluster's mask selects. Dashed vertical guide lines show where the masks overlap. The top bar is annotated '200 selected by mask'. A fourth bar below shows the dark union of all masks, labeled '≈ 3,000 across all masks'. The bottom axis is labeled 'SAE dimension d = 16,384'. The eye goes first to the colored clusters, then follows the dashed lines to the bars.
caption: Per-cluster masks in SAE's feature space. Left: 2D projection of $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with three highlighted clusters. Right: the indices of features selected by the mask $m_c$ for each cluster. Each mask retains $200$ features, and the masks are partially overlapping; their union covers approximately $3{,}000$ features, still much smaller than $d$.
abstract: Deployment-time safety methods for large language models (LLMs) are predominantly supervised and assume access to unsafe training data. Nevertheless, new attacks and harm categories regularly arise, not captured by models trained in such a supervised fashion. An alternative approach is to view this problem through the lens of anomaly detection, namely, to rely solely on modeling safe data and flagging out-of-distribution inputs. However, LLM activations lie in a high-dimensional space, raising concerns about whether anomaly detection is statistically feasible. We show that, under the linear representation hypothesis (LRH), there may indeed be hope. In the LRH concept space, which is typically recovered via a sparse autoencoder (SAE), nearby points share a small common active support. Using this local sparsity insight, we propose a framework for locally masked SAE-based anomaly detection, supported by theoretical justifications. We validate it on various architectures and datasets, including both capability-testing datasets and safety-specific datasets. Finally, when we allow algorithms to use 1% out-of-distribution data for calibration, locally sparse methods achieve near-optimal performance, demonstrating their ability to capture meaningful safety information while using only 1-2% of SAE neurons for computation.
